Ordo Salutis (Doctrine)
OR-doh sa-LOO-tis
noun (Reformed soteriology)
Latin: order of salvation. The Reformed-confessional doctrine of the logical (not necessarily temporal) order of the various aspects of the application of redemption to the believer: effectual calling, regeneration, faith and repentance, justification, adoption, sanctification, perseverance, and glorification.

📖 Biblical Definition

Latin for order of salvation; the Reformed-confessional doctrine of the logical order of the various aspects of the application of redemption to the believer. The ordo salutis distinguishes and orders the several saving works of God in their logical (and to some extent temporal) sequence, as God applies the redemption accomplished by Christ to the elect through the work of the Holy Spirit. The standard Reformed order, drawn principally from Romans 8:29-30 (the golden chain: foreknew, predestinated, called, justified, glorified) and developed in the Reformed-confessional tradition: (1) effectual calling (the Spirit's sovereign, efficacious summons of the elect through the gospel); (2) regeneration (the new birth, the Spirit's implanting of new spiritual life); (3) conversion — faith and repentance (the regenerate sinner's turning to Christ in faith and from sin in repentance); (4) justification (God's forensic declaration of the believer righteous on the basis of Christ's imputed righteousness received through faith); (5) adoption (the believer's reception into the family of God as a son); (6) sanctification (the Spirit's progressive renewal of the believer in holiness); (7) perseverance (the believer's being kept by God's power in faith unto the end); (8) glorification (the final perfecting of the believer in soul and body). The order is principally logical (the steps are distinguished by their logical relations) rather than strictly temporal (several occur simultaneously in the moment of salvation, e.g., calling, regeneration, faith, justification, adoption); regeneration logically precedes faith (the new birth enables the dead sinner to believe, John 3:3; the monergistic principle); justification and adoption are simultaneous with faith; sanctification begins at regeneration and continues throughout life; glorification is the final consummation. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive ordo salutis as a framework for understanding the application of redemption, with regeneration logically prior to faith (against the Arminian ordering that makes faith prior to regeneration); the order displays the monergistic, God-initiated, Spirit-applied character of salvation from first to last.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Latin order of salvation; the Reformed-confessional doctrine of the logical order of the application of redemption: effectual calling, regeneration, faith and repentance, justification, adoption, sanctification, perseverance, glorification; drawn from Romans 8:29-30; principally logical, not strictly temporal; regeneration logically prior to faith (monergism).

ORDO SALUTIS (DOCTRINE), n. (Reformed soteriology; Latin, order of salvation) The logical order of the aspects of the application of redemption to the believer by the Spirit. Standard Reformed order (from Romans 8:29-30, the golden chain): effectual calling, regeneration, conversion (faith and repentance), justification, adoption, sanctification, perseverance, glorification. Principally logical (distinguished by logical relations) rather than strictly temporal (several simultaneous in the moment of salvation). Regeneration logically precedes faith (the new birth enables the dead sinner to believe, John 3:3; monergism), against the Arminian ordering of faith prior to regeneration. Displays the monergistic, God-initiated, Spirit-applied character of salvation from first to last.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 8:29-30 — "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son... Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified."

John 3:3 — "Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God."

1 Corinthians 6:11 — "And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."

Titus 3:5-7 — "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost... That being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The ordo salutis displays the monergistic, Spirit-applied character of salvation; the principal contest is the ordering of regeneration and faith — the Reformed order places regeneration logically prior to faith (monergism), against the Arminian order of faith prior to regeneration (synergism).

expand to see more

The ordo salutis is principally a framework for understanding the application of redemption, and the principal contest concerns the ordering of regeneration and faith. The Reformed order places regeneration logically prior to faith: the sinner is dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), unable to believe of his own fallen nature; the Holy Spirit must first regenerate him (impart new spiritual life, the new birth) before he can exercise saving faith; regeneration is therefore the monergistic work of God that enables and produces the faith of the regenerate sinner (John 3:3, one must be born again to see the kingdom; 1 John 5:1, whosoever believes is born of God, the believing flowing from the being-born). The Arminian order reverses this, placing faith prior to regeneration: the sinner, enabled by prevenient grace, exercises faith of his own cooperating will, and on the basis of that faith is regenerated; this makes regeneration contingent on the sinner's prior faith (synergism). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed ordering: regeneration logically precedes and produces faith; the new birth is the sovereign, monergistic work of the Spirit that raises the dead sinner to life and enables him to believe; salvation is God-initiated and Spirit-applied from first to last. The ordo salutis as a whole displays this monergistic character: every step (calling, regeneration, faith, justification, adoption, sanctification, perseverance, glorification) is the work of God applying to the elect the redemption accomplished by Christ; the believer contributes nothing to the ground of his salvation, which is Christ's finished work received by Spirit-given faith.
